ModelCharacter: The original Swedish Albin pocket cruiser: a narrow, low-powered displacement motorboat with forward and aft cabins, protected center cockpit and a deep keel that gives directional stability while shielding the propeller. It delivers remarkable accommodation and economy for 25 feet.
DesignLineage: Per Brohäll designed the Albin 25 for Albin Marin in Sweden; more than 2,000 were built from the late 1960s into the early 1980s.
The hull was offered as both a pure motor cruiser and a motorsailer; this B-Atlas record represents the motor-cruiser configuration.
The deep keel developed partly for the motorsailer version benefits the motor cruiser through tracking and propeller protection.
The later U.S.-built Albin 27 Family Cruiser was explicitly developed as a descendant of the Swedish Albin 25.
OwnershipCharacter: Exceptionally economical and mechanically simple, with current owner knowledge still abundant. Many boats have been repowered, home-finished or heavily modified, so exact systems and build quality should be verified hull by hull.

ModelCharacter: One of Sea Ray's most enduring model names, but not one continuous boat. The 340 Sundancer appeared in at least three distinct generations—1984–89, 1999–2002 and 2003–08—each a twin-engine planing express with large social cockpit and overnight cabin, but with materially different dimensions, hulls and layouts.
DesignLineage: The first major 340 Sundancer generation ran from 1984–1989.
Sea Ray revived the 340 Sundancer name for an all-new 1999–2002 generation.
A substantially larger redesigned 340 followed for 2003–2008 with 12-foot beam and different cockpit/hull architecture.
The repeated model name should never be treated as a single continuous hull family; listing year is essential to identity.
OwnershipCharacter: Broad dealer knowledge and mass-market parts support are advantages, but ownership varies strongly by generation and drivetrain. Twin gasoline engines are common and fuel-intensive; sterndrive examples add drive/bellows maintenance, while inboard boats trade efficiency for simpler underwater gear.

Strengths: Revolutionary hull geometry offers completely flat running angles, exceptional efficiency across all speed bands, premium build quality
Weaknesses: Extremely rare production numbers make sourcing difficult, unusual underwater profile requires care when blocking.
CommonProblems: Electronic trim tab sync sensor errors, localized raw water strainer mounting bracket vibrations.
TypicalMission: Fast tactical coastal adventuring, fuel-efficient waterway tracking, and weekend gunkholing.
AvoidIf: You prefer a traditional heavy-displacement profile or expansive multi-room accommodations

ModelCharacter: A radical Walter Schulz powerboat built around his patented SRD—Schulz Reverse Deadrise—hull, intended to provide planing-boat speed with a softer, more stable ride than conventional hard-chine V-bottoms. DesignLineage: Walter Schulz developed the patented SRD hull after decades of Shannon sail and powerboat building.
The 38 SRD was the first widely documented production expression of the concept in the mid-2000s.

ModelVariations.Name: Later 34 Outboard Express
ModelVariations.Description: A later/revived True North 34 Outboard Express uses twin gasoline outboards and materially different performance; it should be treated as a distinct generation/model record rather than overwriting the original diesel 34.

ModelCharacter: The original True North 34 is a minimalist New England cruising boat evolved from the 2003 True North 33: plumb bow, large cockpit, opening transom, resin-infused construction and a single inboard diesel deliver a distinctive mix of lobsterboat character, rough-water ability and deliberately low-maintenance cruising.
DesignLineage: Everett Pearson introduced the True North 38 in 2001 and the smaller True North 33 in 2003.
Later modifications to the 33's transom increased overall length and the model became the True North 34.
The original 34 normally used a single 370-hp inboard diesel.

In 2015 a twin-outboard version appeared, and Catalina later revived the design as the True North 34 Outboard Express; B-Atlas's current record specifically represents the earlier diesel/inboard generation.
OwnershipCharacter: A deliberately simple cruising concept with minimal exterior brightwork, large utility cockpit and single-diesel machinery. Resin-infused construction and restrained systems help ownership, but discontinued-original-builder parts and the evolution through several corporate owners mean model-specific support is less direct than for a current Fortier.

Overview: The Willard 40 Vega Nomad belongs to Willard Marine’s early production-fiberglass cruising lineage. These heavy, economical boats use displacement hulls and simple diesel propulsion, with the Vega families offered in materially different sedan, pilothouse and motorsailer configurations.

CoupleCruising.Summary: The documented layout and cruising systems are well suited to a cruising couple, with guest capacity varying by model.

SoloHandling.Summary: Protected helms and deck access can support short-handed operation, but displacement, windage, engine arrangement and docking equipment vary materially by model.

InlandWaterways.Summary: Route suitability depends on beam, draft and actual air draft; larger models may face marina and lock constraints.

ExposedWater.Summary: Hull form and construction support the documented cruising role, but condition, loading, weather and individual configuration remain decisive.

ModelVariations.Name: Vega configuration families
ModelVariations.Description: Willard used the same hull families for distinct Nomad, Voyager, Horizon, Searcher and other configurations. “Vega” identifies a hull family rather than one universal layout.

ModelCharacter: An exceptionally rare widebody flybridge sedan from Willard's early Vega 40 family, using a full-displacement hull, two-stateroom/two-head interior and no side decks to maximize living space in a traditional long-range cruiser.
DesignLineage: The Vega 40 was introduced in 1973 as the larger replacement for the Vega 36.
The early 1973–1977 Vega 40 family consisted of Nomad flybridge sedans, Voyager raised-pilothouse boats and one motorsailer.
Only three Vega 40 Nomads were built, and the Nomad used a widebody salon without walkaround side decks.
In 1977 Willard replaced the early Vega 40 with a new molded-superstructure 40; the later Flybridge Sedan regained side decks and should not be conflated with the Vega 40 Nomad.
OwnershipCharacter: Large living space and full-displacement efficiency are attractive, but scarcity means nearly every assumption must be verified on the individual hull. Lack of side decks, vintage systems, plywood-era superstructure construction and limited model-specific parts make condition more important than nominal specification.
